title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals deployed deepfake and voice-cloning AI technology to impersonate real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney, in order to defraud victims. The scams operated on social media and through phone calls targeting immigrants and other vulnerable populations. The impersonations worked because victims had no way to verify they were communicating with the real person rather than an AI replica.

The deployment failure was the absence of any authentication mechanism between the scammer and the victim. Deepfake technology created convincing enough replicas that victims sent money based on fabricated video, audio, or phone calls. A verification system, such as pre-established code words or independent confirmation through a known contact method, could have caught the impersonation before victims lost funds.

It is not established whether the AI systems used to create these deepfakes were purpose-built fraud tools or whether criminals repurposed commercial AI products. The reports document the scale of losses but do not establish the technical origin or capabilities of the systems involved.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit sophisticated scams across Georgia and South Florida. They employ deepfake technology to clone voices, create fake photos, and spoof phone numbers to impersonate trusted individuals. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were stolen to target immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year, with over 1 million total internet crime complaints resulting in more than $20 billion in reported losses.

Florida and Georgia have been hit particularly hard, with Florida reporting 350 AI-related complaints and nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints totaling over $10.4 million. Common scams include voice-cloning schemes targeting grandparents and romance scams. Authorities warn these figures likely undercount the actual problem since many victims never report crimes. To protect themselves, consumers should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests through known phone numbers, avoid sending money based on calls alone, and report suspected scams to law enforcement.
